scope: Translation decisions, transmission errors and interpolations that measurably changed Christian doctrine, practice, art or law. Each case is anchored to verse references that resolve against the version files in this repository.
method: Every case names (a) the source-language reading, (b) the rendering that departed from it, (c) the witnesses in THIS repository that attest each side, and (d) a consensus grade. Witness lists are deliberately incomplete: they name versions sufficient to see the contrast, not every version that agrees.

taxonomy.lexical-error: The receiving language word does not mean what the source word means.
taxonomy.semantic-narrowing: A source word with a broad or ambiguous range is rendered by a narrower word, foreclosing readings the original left open.
taxonomy.grammatical-misreading: Case, mood, syntax or punctuation is construed in a way the source does not support.
taxonomy.textual-interpolation: Words absent from the earliest witnesses entered the text and were then translated as scripture.
taxonomy.vocalization-variant: An unpointed consonantal Hebrew text was vocalized one way rather than another, changing the sense.
taxonomy.transliteration-as-name: A common noun or epithet was carried over as if it were a proper name.
taxonomy.anachronism: A term was rendered with a concept that did not exist when the text was written.
taxonomy.interpretive-gloss: The rendering imports a later doctrinal reading rather than translating the words.
taxonomy.folk-etymology: A popular claim of mistranslation that scholarship does not support. Included so the dataset can be used to test claims, not only to confirm them.
taxonomy.scribal-harmonization: A scribe altered wording to remove a theological difficulty. Distinguished from textual-interpolation by motive and shape: nothing is added, a word is swapped for a safer one.

consensus_levels.strong: Broad agreement across confessional lines that the rendering departs from the source.
consensus_levels.majority: Most critical scholars agree; a reasoned minority defends the traditional rendering.
consensus_levels.contested: Live scholarly dispute; the dataset records the dispute, not a verdict.
consensus_levels.debunked: The popular 'mistranslation' claim fails on the evidence.

cases.title: eph' hō -> 'in quo': all sinned 'in Adam'

source_term.gloss: because / inasmuch as

cases.what_happened: Paul writes that death spread to all 'eph' hō all sinned' - a causal construction meaning 'because all sinned'. The Old Latin and Vulgate rendered it 'in quo', 'in whom', making Adam the antecedent, so that all humanity is said to have sinned inside Adam.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Augustine built the doctrine of inherited guilt on the Latin reading, against Pelagius. Seminal transmission of guilt, infant baptism as remission of inherited sin, and the Western doctrine of original sin all lean on 'in quo'. The Greek East, reading the Greek, developed inherited mortality rather than inherited guilt - the single largest doctrinal divergence between Eastern and Western Christianity traceable to one preposition.
cases.caveat: That 'in quo' is not what the Greek says is near-universally granted; whether Augustine's doctrine actually depends on it, or merely found support in it, is debated. Some read eph' hō as 'on the basis of which' or even 'on which condition'. The English split is now datable: Geneva 1599 reads 'in who all men haue sinned', carrying the Latin; Tyndale 1526 reads 'in somoche that all men synned', which is the causal sense of the Greek. Tyndale, working from Erasmus, got there seventy years earlier. Wycliffe (1395) is now the earliest English witness and carries the Latin straight through: 'deth passide forth in to alle men, in whic alle men synneden'.
scholarship: Joseph A. Fitzmyer, Romans (Anchor Bible, 1993) - on eph' ho and the Latin rendering.
Peter Brown, Augustine of Hippo: A Biography, rev. ed. (California, 2000).

cases.title: qāran -> 'cornuta': the horned Moses

source_term.gloss: sent out rays, shone

cases.what_happened: The Hebrew verb qāran is denominative from qeren, 'horn', and in this context means that Moses' face emitted beams of light. Jerome rendered it literally as 'horned'.
cases.doctrinal_impact: A millennium of Western art depicted Moses with horns - Michelangelo's Moses in San Pietro in Vincoli is the famous case. The image was later attached to an antisemitic trope of horned Jews in medieval and early-modern Europe. A rare case where the downstream effect was iconographic and social rather than doctrinal.
cases.caveat: CORRECTED after checking the standard monograph. Ruth Mellinkoff's 'The Horned Moses in Medieval Art and Thought' (1970) argues that Jerome most likely intended 'cornuta' as a metaphor for Moses' newly evident POWER, not as an error and not as a slur: horns signified divine authority across the ancient Near East, and horned headgear marked priests and kings. She distinguishes medieval 'horns of honour' from 'horns of dishonour' and treats the antisemitic reading as a later development rather than the origin. The earlier version of this case overstated the causal chain: the Vulgate reading is real and the art tradition is real, but 'the mistranslation caused the antisemitic trope' is not what the definitive study concludes. The Septuagint had already read it as glorification (dedoxastai), showing the radiance reading was available to Jerome.
scholarship: Ruth Mellinkoff, The Horned Moses in Medieval Art and Thought (University of California Press, 1970) - the standard monograph, and it qualifies this case rather than supporting it.

cases.title: The Comma Johanneum: a Trinity proof-text that entered late

source_term.gloss: for there are three that testify

rendered_as.form: ... ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ, ὁ πατήρ, ὁ λόγος, καὶ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα
rendered_as.gloss: ... in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit

cases.what_happened: The heavenly-witnesses clause appears in no Greek manuscript before the 14th century and in no Greek Father during the Trinitarian controversies. It began as a Latin gloss, migrated into the Vulgate tradition, and entered the printed Greek text when Erasmus admitted it under pressure after omitting it from his first two editions. From the Textus Receptus it passed into the KJV.
cases.doctrinal_impact: For three centuries the most-quoted scriptural proof of the Trinity in English-speaking Protestantism was a verse that is not in the New Testament. Its removal from the Revised Version onward became a flashpoint of the King-James-Only movement and a standard case study in why textual criticism matters for doctrine.

first_attested.where: Latin tradition; Greek MSS only from the 14th c.

cases.caveat: This repository is unusually good for this case: the Byzantine Majority Text omits the Comma while the two Textus Receptus editions include it, so the contrast is visible inside the Greek files alone. Wycliffe 1395 carries the Comma into English from the Vulgate, four generations before Erasmus admitted it to the printed Greek - which is the clearest demonstration that it reached English through Latin, not through Greek manuscripts.

distinguish_from.note: The Comma was the most-quoted English proof-text for three centuries, but the doctrine was defined at Nicaea and Constantinople by Greek-speaking bishops whose manuscripts did not contain it. Removing it removes a proof-text, not the doctrine.

scholarship: Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd ed. (UBS, 1994), on 1 John 5:7-8 - traces the clause to a 4th-century Latin treatise and its entry into Vulgate MSS from the 6th century.

cases.title: metanoeite -> 'paenitentiam agite': repent or do penance

source_term.gloss: change your mind, turn around inwardly

cases.what_happened: Jerome rendered the inward metanoeite with a phrase that names an outward act. Over centuries 'paenitentiam agite' was read as a command to perform the acts of the sacrament of penance.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Arguably the single most consequential translation decision in Western history. Erasmus' 1516 annotation - that the Greek means 'resipiscite', change your mind - reached Luther, whose Ninety-Five Theses open by declaring that when Christ said 'poenitentiam agite' he willed the whole life of believers to be repentance, not the sacrament of penance. The indulgence controversy, and with it the Reformation, starts at this word.
cases.caveat: Catholic scholars note that 'paenitentiam agere' could carry a broader sense of 'be penitent' in Jerome's Latin, and that the penitential system did not derive from this verse alone. The historical effect is not in dispute. Now visible end to end in English: Wycliffe (1395), translating the Vulgate, reads 'Do ye penaunce'; Tyndale (1526), translating Erasmus' Greek, reads 'repent'; Geneva (1599) reads 'Amende your liues'. The Reformation's central exegetical claim is legible as a change of two English words between two translations.
scholarship: David Daniell, The Bible in English: Its History and Influence (Yale, 2003).
Erika Rummel, Erasmus' Annotations on the New Testament (Toronto, 1986).

cases.title: hêlēl ben-shachar -> 'Lucifer': how Satan got a name

source_term.gloss: shining one, son of the dawn (the morning star)

cases.what_happened: The passage is a taunt-song against the king of Babylon, using morning-star imagery for a ruler who overreached. Latin 'lucifer' was an ordinary noun for the morning star, and the Vulgate used it as such. English versions capitalised it, turning a common noun in a Babylonian dirge into a personal name for the devil.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Produced the entire Western narrative of Satan's pre-creation fall from heaven, a story the Bible never tells in those terms. Milton's Paradise Lost, medieval demonology, and popular Christian cosmology all rest on reading Isaiah 14 as Satan's biography. Note that Revelation 22:16 calls Jesus the morning star, using the same image the tradition assigned to the devil.

first_attested.where: Vulgate; the personal-name reading from patristic exegesis onward

cases.caveat: The identification of Isaiah 14 with Satan predates the Vulgate (it is in Origen and Tertullian), so the Latin word reinforced an existing reading rather than creating it from nothing. The capitalisation in English is what fixed it as a proper name. Geneva 1599 already reads 'O Lucifer, sonne of the morning', so the capitalised proper name entered English at least twelve years before the KJV. Wycliffe 1395 - 'A! Lucifer, that risidist eerli' - is the earliest English witness. The split is not chronological but confessional and text-critical: Leeser's Jewish translation reads 'O morning-star' in 1853 and Rotherham 'O Shining One' in 1902, while Darby and Noyes keep 'Lucifer' in the same period.

distinguish_from.note: The fall motif has New Testament texts of its own. What Isaiah 14:12 supplied was the devil's name and a pre-creation backstory, neither of which is in those texts.

scholarship: Joseph Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39 (Anchor Bible, 2000).
Jeffrey Burton Russell, The Devil: Perceptions of Evil from Antiquity to Primitive Christianity (Cornell, 1977).

cases.title: Junia -> 'Junias': the apostle who was edited into a man

source_term.gloss: Junia, a common Roman woman's name

rendered_as.gloss: Junias, a man's name otherwise unattested

cases.what_happened: Paul greets Andronicus and Junia, 'outstanding among the apostles'. Unaccented Greek leaves the name ambiguous; when scribes began accenting in the 7th century they wrote the feminine. Every ancient commentator read a woman. From 1927 a leading critical edition printed the masculine accent, and English versions followed with 'Junias' - a name with no attestation anywhere in Greek or Latin antiquity, against 250-plus inscriptions for Junia.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Removed the New Testament's only named female apostle from the text for most of the 20th century, at precisely the period when women's ordination was being debated. The reversal in NA27/28 and in NRSV, ESV and NIV restored her, and the case is now a standard exhibit for how translator assumptions enter the text.

first_attested.where: Luther's German NT; standardised by Nestle 1927

cases.caveat: A second question rides along: whether 'episēmoi en tois apostolois' means 'outstanding among the apostles' (she was one) or 'well known to the apostles' (she was not). That is a genuinely open grammatical dispute; the sex of the name is not. The mid-20th-century versions that printed 'Junias' are not in this repository, so the shift itself is only partly visible here.
scholarship: Eldon Jay Epp, Junia: The First Woman Apostle (Fortress, 2005) - the standard treatment, tracing the masculinisation through manuscripts, accentuation and modern critical editions.

cases.title: 'almāh -> parthenos: the virgin of Isaiah 7:14

source_term.gloss: young woman of marriageable age

cases.what_happened: Hebrew has a specific word for virgin, bethulah; Isaiah used 'almāh, which marks age and social status rather than sexual history. The Septuagint chose parthenos, which in ordinary Greek means virgin. Matthew quotes the Greek, not the Hebrew, as proof of the virgin birth.
cases.doctrinal_impact: The scriptural anchor of the virgin birth, and by extension of Mariology. When the RSV printed 'young woman' in 1952 the reaction was ferocious - copies were burned from pulpits - and the controversy directly motivated the founding of evangelical translation projects that became the NASB and NIV. Modern Bible-translation politics begins here.
cases.caveat: Not a clean error. Most scholars hold 'young woman' is the better rendering, but 'almāh does not exclude virginity, and an unmarried young woman would ordinarily be presumed a virgin. Best described as interpretive narrowing that later bore enormous doctrinal weight. Matthew's argument depends on the Greek, so for Matthew 1:23 'virgin' is simply correct. MAJOR CORRECTION on the evidence now in this repository: the RSV did not introduce 'young woman' into English in 1952. Leeser's Jewish translation reads 'this young woman' in 1853, Noyes reads 'the damsel' in 1869, and the Bible in Basic English reads 'a young woman' in 1949 - three English versions with the non-virgin reading, spanning a century before the RSV. The 1952 controversy was not about a novel rendering; it was about that rendering appearing in a mainline pulpit Bible.

distinguish_from.note: Luke and Matthew were written in Greek; there is no Hebrew original behind them. Luke 1:34 has Mary say 'I do not know a man' in the author's own idiom. The doctrine is independent of Isaiah 7:14. What the Septuagint's rendering produced is the prophecy - the claim that the Hebrew Bible foretold a virgin birth - not the belief itself.

scholarship: Peter J. Thuesen, In Discordance with the Scriptures: American Protestant Battles over Translating the Bible (Oxford, 1999) - on the RSV controversy this verse triggered.

cases.title: malakoi / arsenokoitai -> 'homosexuals' (1946)

source_term.gloss: soft ones ... male-bedders (a Pauline coinage, probably from Leviticus 18:22 LXX)

cases.what_happened: The 1946 RSV New Testament collapsed two distinct Greek words into the single modern noun 'homosexuals'. No prior translation in any language had done so - earlier English versions used behavioural phrases, and the concept of sexual orientation did not exist until the late 19th century.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Turned texts about acts into a text about a category of person, which is how the verse then functioned in 20th-century church discipline, ordination bans and civil legislation. Later RSV-family editions retreated: the RSV itself revised in 1971, and the 2021 NRSVue renders 'male prostitutes' and 'men who engage in illicit sex'.
cases.caveat: Genuinely contested. That 'homosexuals' is an anachronism is widely granted even by traditionalist scholars; that the underlying Greek therefore does not condemn same-sex acts is not. The popular framing - that one 1946 decision created Christian homophobia - overstates a real translation problem, since Leviticus and Romans 1 were read restrictively long before 1946. The RSV 1946 itself is not in this repository, so the moment of the shift can only be inferred here from before-and-after versions. Verified here: the NASB family and the NET all use 'homosexual' language, while the KJV, ASV and NRSV use behavioural phrases ('abusers of themselves with mankind', 'male prostitutes, sodomites') - so in this repository the oldest and the newest versions land on the same side and the mid-century ones do not.

distinguish_from.note: These texts were read restrictively long before 1946, which is why the popular framing - that one translation decision created Christian homophobia - overstates a real translation problem. The 1946 rendering changed the register from acts to identity; it did not originate the prohibition.

scholarship: Dale B. Martin, Sex and the Single Savior: Gender and Sexuality in Biblical Interpretation (Westminster John Knox, 2006) - includes his essay on arsenokoites and malakos.
Anthony C. Thiselton, The First Epistle to the Corinthians (NIGTC, Eerdmans, 2000) - surveys the lexical debate from the other side.

cases.title: hu' -> 'ipsa': she shall crush the serpent's head

source_term.gloss: he / it (masculine, agreeing with 'seed')

cases.what_happened: The Hebrew pronoun is masculine and refers back to the woman's seed. Clementine Vulgate manuscripts read 'ipsa conteret caput tuum' - 'she shall crush thy head' - making Eve, and typologically Mary, the one who crushes the serpent.
cases.doctrinal_impact: The textual basis for the Marian reading of the protoevangelium and for the ubiquitous image of Mary standing on a serpent. Cited in the 1854 bull Ineffabilis Deus defining the Immaculate Conception. The Nova Vulgata of 1979 restored 'ipsum'.
cases.caveat: Whether Jerome himself wrote 'ipsa' or it entered in transmission is disputed; his commentary on Isaiah shows he knew the Hebrew is masculine. Modern Catholic scholarship does not defend 'ipsa' as a translation, only the typology it came to carry. This case is now as close to settled as the dataset gets. FOUR independent ancient traditions read a masculine subject: the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch (a Hebrew tradition separate from the Jewish one since c. 200 BCE), the Septuagint, and Targum Onkelos. Only the Latin reads a feminine - and it does so in BOTH official printed editions, the Sixtine of 1590 and the Clementine of 1592, so this was not a stray printing. Wycliffe then carried it into English as 'sche schal breke thin heed'.
scholarship: Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11: A Commentary (Fortress, 1984).
Marina Warner, Alone of All Her Sex: The Myth and the Cult of the Virgin Mary (Knopf, 1976).

cases.title: mystērion -> 'sacramentum': marriage becomes a sacrament

source_term.gloss: mystery, something previously hidden now disclosed

rendered_as.gloss: sacred sign / oath; later, a channel of grace

cases.what_happened: Latin rendered mystērion as sacramentum throughout. The Greek word means a revealed secret; the Latin word acquired, over centuries, the technical sense of an efficacious rite. Paul's statement that marriage is a great 'mystery' was read as a statement that marriage is a sacrament.
cases.doctrinal_impact: A principal scriptural support for numbering marriage among the seven sacraments, affirmed at Trent. Erasmus' annotation that mystērion does not mean sacramentum was among the passages the Reformers seized on, and Protestant rejection of marriage as a sacrament follows the Greek.
cases.caveat: In the 4th century 'sacramentum' was a reasonable equivalent; the drift happened in the Latin word, not at the moment of translation. This is a case of a translation aging badly rather than being wrong when made. Tyndale and Geneva both read 'a great secrete', refusing the sacramental vocabulary outright. The Reformation's rejection of marriage as a sacrament is visible in the word choice itself.
scholarship: Ernest Best, Ephesians (ICC, T&T Clark, 1998).

cases.title: kecharitōmenē -> 'gratia plena': full of grace

source_term.gloss: having been favoured / graced (perfect passive participle)

cases.what_happened: The participle says Mary has been the recipient of favour. The Latin 'gratia plena' suggests a quantity of grace filling her, which supported reading the verse as a statement about Mary's interior condition rather than about God's action toward her.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Embedded in the Ave Maria and thus in the daily devotional life of Western Christendom. Used in the development of Mary's sinlessness and, eventually, the Immaculate Conception. Erasmus' rendering 'gratiosa' was condemned at the Sorbonne - a small philological point that became a confessional battle line.
cases.caveat: 'Full of grace' is defensible as dynamic equivalence; the perfect passive does imply a completed, abiding state. The dispute is over how much theological weight the participle can carry, not over a flat error. Wycliffe and Tyndale both read 'full of grace'; Geneva 1599 breaks with them - 'Haile thou that art freely beloued' - which is close to what modern critical versions do, four centuries early.
scholarship: Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Gospel According to Luke I-IX (Anchor Bible, 1981).
Marina Warner, Alone of All Her Sex (Knopf, 1976).

cases.title: 'tree of life' -> 'book of life': Erasmus back-translates the Vulgate

source_term.gloss: the tree of life

rendered_as.form: τῆς βίβλου τῆς ζωῆς / the book of life

cases.what_happened: Erasmus' only Greek manuscript of Revelation lacked the final leaf, so he retranslated the last six verses from Latin back into Greek. His reconstruction produced readings found in no Greek manuscript at all, including 'book of life' for 'tree of life'.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Made the Bible's closing warning appear to threaten erasure from the book of life - a soteriological threat - rather than loss of access to the tree of life. More broadly it is the clearest demonstration that the Textus Receptus behind the KJV contains readings with zero Greek manuscript support, which is why this verse recurs in every debate over Bible versions.
cases.caveat: The Latin itself reflects a real variant tradition; Erasmus did not invent the reading so much as enshrine it in Greek. Note that the Vulgate here is a witness to the shifted reading.
scholarship: Bruce M. Metzger and Bart D. Ehrman, The Text of the New Testament, 4th ed. (Oxford, 2005) - on Erasmus' back-translation of the final leaf.

cases.title: pascha -> 'Easter' (KJV only)

source_term.gloss: Passover

rendered_as.gloss: the Christian feast of the Resurrection

cases.what_happened: The KJV renders pascha as 'Passover' in its other 28 New Testament occurrences and as 'Easter' only here, describing Herod's intentions in a thoroughly Jewish setting years before a Christian Easter observance existed.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Small in itself, historically outsized: it is the stock example in arguments about KJV inerrancy, and it has been used to argue both that Easter is apostolic and that the KJV is uniquely reliable or uniquely flawed. A clean demonstration that a single word can carry a whole controversy.
cases.caveat: In early modern English 'Easter' could still denote the paschal season generally, so the KJV translators were less obviously wrong than they look now. The NKJV's silent correction is itself informative. Verified here: Webster's 1833 revision of the KJV silently reads 'the passover', so the correction was being made in the KJV's own line of descent nearly two centuries before the NKJV. CORRECTION: the rendering originates with Tyndale (1526), who reads 'entendynge after ester'. More striking, Geneva 1599 had already corrected it to 'after the Passeouer' - so the KJV translators had the right reading in front of them and reverted to Tyndale's. That makes this a deliberate choice rather than an oversight.
scholarship: David Daniell, The Bible in English (Yale, 2003).
David Daniell, William Tyndale: A Biography (Yale, 1994).

cases.title: The Longer Ending of Mark

source_term.gloss: for they were afraid (where Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end)

rendered_as.gloss: twelve further verses of resurrection appearances and signs

cases.what_happened: The two oldest complete Greek Bibles end Mark at 16:8; Eusebius and Jerome report that accurate copies lacked what follows. The longer ending differs from Mark in vocabulary and style and exists in several competing forms.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Verse 18 - taking up serpents and drinking deadly poison - is the scriptural basis of Appalachian snake-handling churches, a practice with a documented death toll that rests on twelve verses most text critics regard as secondary. The passage also carries a baptismal-salvation formula (16:16) used in sacramental debates.

first_attested.where: 2nd c. CE appendix; absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus

cases.caveat: Not a mistranslation but a transmission event, included because the doctrinal and practical effects are of the same kind. Warning: this repository's version files carry no textual apparatus, so versions that bracket or footnote these verses are indistinguishable here from versions that print them as plain text. Verify against a critical edition before drawing conclusions from the JSON alone.
scholarship: Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, pp. 122-126 - the UBS committee printed the verses in double square brackets to mark them as by a hand other than the evangelist.

cases.title: The woman taken in adultery

source_term.gloss: the earliest Greek witnesses move from John 7:52 to 8:12

cases.what_happened: The passage is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts, unknown to the Greek commentators on John, and appears at four different locations in the manuscripts that do carry it - including after Luke 21:38. Its style is closer to Luke than to John.
cases.doctrinal_impact: 'Let him who is without sin cast the first stone' is among the most widely known sentences attributed to Jesus and has shaped Christian teaching on judgment, mercy and capital punishment far out of proportion to its textual standing. A case where a probably non-original passage became load-bearing for Christian ethics.
cases.caveat: Many scholars who judge it non-Johannine still regard the story as early and plausibly historical. As with Mark 16, the repository's plain-text JSON cannot show which versions bracket the passage.
scholarship: Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, on John 7:53-8:11.

cases.title: 'money is the root of all evil'

source_term.form: ῥίζα ... πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία
source_term.translit: rhiza ... pantōn tōn kakōn estin hē philarguria
source_term.gloss: a root of all kinds of evils is the love of money

rendered_as.form: the root of all evil is money
rendered_as.gloss: money itself is the sole source of evil

cases.what_happened: The Greek has an anarthrous 'a root', and the subject is philarguria, love of money, not money. The KJV's word order - 'the love of money is the root of all evil' - is defensible, but the sentence detached from its context and became the proverb 'money is the root of all evil'.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Shaped centuries of Christian attitudes to wealth and commerce, and supplied the proverb that most English speakers can quote and most misattribute. Included as the clearest case of a rendering that is nearly right but whose downstream popular form is flatly wrong.
cases.caveat: The KJV is not really mistranslating; the popular proverb is. Useful as a control case: it tests whether an analysis pipeline can distinguish a translation problem from a reception problem. Tyndale reads 'coveteousnes is the rote of all evyll' and Geneva 'the desire of money is the roote of all euill' - both keep the subject on the desire rather than the money.
scholarship: I. Howard Marshall, The Pastoral Epistles (ICC, T&T Clark, 1999).

cases.title: mekhashēphāh -> 'witch': the text used at the witch trials

source_term.gloss: female practitioner of kishuf - sorcery, incantation, possibly poisoning

rendered_as.gloss: a woman in league with the devil

cases.what_happened: The Hebrew names a specific illicit ritual practitioner within Israel's cultic law. English 'witch' in 1611 carried the fully developed demonological meaning of the early modern period: a person in pact with Satan. The Septuagint's 'pharmakous' points toward potion-makers, a different picture again.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Directly invoked in early modern witch prosecutions across Europe and in New England; King James himself wrote Daemonologie and the KJV rendering hardened a legal category. Tens of thousands of executions cited this verse. The clearest case in the dataset where a lexical choice has a body count.

first_attested.where: English versions from the 16th c.; fixed by the KJV

cases.caveat: The scholarly dispute is over the semantic range of kishuf, not over whether 'witch' imports early modern baggage - that much is agreed. The causal claim about the trials is also contested by historians who note that the persecutions were driven by demonological treatises and legal procedure at least as much as by this verse. CORRECTION, on the evidence now in this repository: 'witch' is not a KJV coinage. Wycliffe (1395) reads 'Thou schalt not suffre witchis to lyue' and Geneva (1599) has the KJV's exact sentence, 'Thou shalt not suffer a witch to liue'. The KJV inherited the wording; the English tradition had settled on it two centuries earlier, well before King James wrote Daemonologie. Leeser's Jewish translation also reads 'a witch' in 1853, so the rendering was not confessionally specific. Rotherham's 'A sorceress' (1902) and the BBE's 'Any woman using unnatural powers' (1949) show the retreat from the demonological word. The Targum is not cited here: its Exodus is offset by one verse.
scholarship: Nahum M. Sarna, The JPS Torah Commentary: Exodus (JPS, 1991) - on mekhashephah within the covenant code.
Brian P. Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe, 4th ed. (Routledge, 2016) - on how far scriptural warrant actually drove the prosecutions.

cases.title: rātsach -> 'kill' rather than 'murder'

source_term.gloss: you shall not commit unlawful killing / murder

cases.what_happened: Hebrew has several verbs for killing; rātsach is the narrow one, used of unlawful killing and manslaughter, never of judicial execution, warfare, or sacrifice - all of which the same legal corpus commands. 'Kill' flattens the distinction.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Framed Christian debates on capital punishment, just war, pacifism, suicide and abortion in English for four centuries. Quaker and Anabaptist pacifism, and modern pro-life argument, both lean on the broad rendering; the shift to 'murder' in most 20th-century versions changed the terms of those debates.
cases.caveat: A minority argues rātsach is broader than 'murder' because it covers negligent homicide, so 'murder' overcorrects. 'Kill' is nonetheless too broad.
scholarship: Wilma Ann Bailey, 'You Shall Not Kill' or 'You Shall Not Murder'? The Assault on a Biblical Text (Liturgical Press, 2005) - a book-length treatment of exactly this case.
Nahum M. Sarna, The JPS Torah Commentary: Exodus (JPS, 1991).

cases.title: authentein -> 'usurp authority' / 'have authority'

source_term.gloss: uncertain; attested senses include to dominate, to act on one's own authority, and in some sources to murder

rendered_as.form: to have authority / to usurp authority

cases.what_happened: The verb is a New Testament hapax and rare in surrounding Greek literature, with a semantic range that does not map onto neutral 'exercise authority'. Translating it as the ordinary word for holding office turns a prohibition on a specific kind of domineering into a prohibition on women in office.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Together with 1 Corinthians 14:34, the central text in every denominational fight over women's ordination. The KJV's 'usurp authority' and the NIV's 'assume authority' (2011) permit narrower readings than the ESV's 'exercise authority', and translation committees have been openly lobbied over this verb.
cases.caveat: 'Shifted' and 'corrected' are not neutral labels here and the dataset flags this case as contested for that reason. Serious scholars defend both renderings; the evidence base is a handful of occurrences in Greek literature spanning centuries. Verified here: the KJV's 'usurp authority' and the NIV 2011's 'assume authority' permit a narrower reading, while the ESV, NASB, CSB, NRSV and NET all use the ordinary office language. The split does not track conservative against progressive, which is itself the point.
scholarship: I. Howard Marshall, The Pastoral Epistles (ICC, 1999) - surveys the lexical evidence for authentein from both sides of the debate.

cases.title: 'ēzer kenegdo -> 'help meet' / 'helper'

source_term.gloss: a strength/help corresponding to him, facing him as an equal

rendered_as.form: an help meet for him / a suitable helper

cases.what_happened: 'Ēzer is used of God as Israel's help sixteen of its twenty-one occurrences in the Hebrew Bible, carrying no note of subordination. Kenegdo means 'corresponding to, opposite him'. English 'helper' imported a subordinate role, and the KJV's 'help meet' was misread as a compound noun, producing the English word 'helpmeet'.
cases.doctrinal_impact: A pillar of complementarian theology and of centuries of argument for women's subordination as the creation order. Feminist and egalitarian biblical scholarship from the 1970s onward made this phrase a primary battleground, and several recent versions have moved toward 'partner' or 'corresponding to him'.

first_attested.where: Greek and Latin, hardened in English

cases.caveat: 'Helper' is not wrong, only underdetermined; the argument is about what English connotations it carries. Not every scholar accepts that kenegdo implies equality. Note that the JPS TANAKH 1917 reproduces the KJV's 'help meet' exactly, so this is not a Christian-versus-Jewish divergence - the versions that render kenegdo as 'partner' or 'counterpart' are all recent.
scholarship: Phyllis Trible, God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality (Fortress, 1978) - the landmark study of this phrase.

cases.title: kā'ărî / kā'ărû -> 'they pierced my hands and feet'

source_term.gloss: like a lion, my hands and my feet (Masoretic vocalization)

rendered_as.gloss: they dug/pierced my hands and my feet

cases.what_happened: The consonantal text can be vocalized kā'ărî ('like a lion') or kā'ărû (a verb). The Masoretic tradition points it as 'lion'; the Septuagint read a verb of digging or piercing. A Nahal Hever scroll fragment supports a verbal reading, so this is a genuine ancient textual divergence rather than a simple error.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Became the Old Testament's most cited prophecy of the crucifixion, and a centrepiece of Christian-Jewish polemic from the patristic period through medieval disputations. Jewish and Christian Bibles print materially different texts at this verse to this day.
cases.caveat: Calling either reading the 'mistranslation' is tendentious, which is why the consensus grade is contested. The Dead Sea Scrolls evidence that bears on it is not in this repository - see the coverage report. Leeser 1853 and Noyes 1869 both print 'like lions', following the Masoretic vocalization, while Rotherham and Darby print 'pierced'. The split runs between translators of the same generation reading the same consonants.

distinguish_from.note: The crucifixion narrative is independent of Psalm 22:16. The disputed vocalization bears on whether the Hebrew Bible prophesied it, not on whether the Gospels report it.

scholarship: Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012).
John Goldingay, Psalms, vol. 1 (Baker Academic, 2006).

cases.title: 'sons of God' -> 'sons of Israel'

source_term.gloss: sons of God (divine beings)

cases.what_happened: The Septuagint and a Qumran Hebrew fragment read that God apportioned the nations according to the number of the 'sons of God'; the Masoretic Text reads 'sons of Israel'. The majority view is that the Masoretic reading is a theological correction smoothing over an older assignment of nations to subordinate divine beings.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Bears directly on how Israelite religion developed from a divine-council cosmology toward strict monotheism, and on New Testament and Second Temple thinking about the powers behind the nations. The reading chosen determines whether the Bible's own text preserves a stage before monotheism.
cases.caveat: The direction of the change is inferred, not observed; a minority holds the Masoretic reading original. The Qumran witness is decisive for most scholars and is absent from this repository, but Brenton and Swete let you see the Septuagint side. New evidence here, and it cuts against the majority view: the Samaritan Pentateuch - an independent Hebrew tradition - also reads 'sons of Israel'. So the Hebrew manuscript traditions agree with each other and the Greek stands alone, which is the opposite of the pattern at Genesis 3:15. Anyone using this dataset should notice that the same kind of argument points different ways at these two verses.
scholarship: Emanuel Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. (Fortress, 2012).
Jeffrey H. Tigay, The JPS Torah Commentary: Deuteronomy (JPS, 1996).

cases.title: Sheol, Hades, Gehenna and Tartarus all rendered 'hell'

source_term.gloss: the grave or realm of the dead; the Greek underworld; the Valley of Hinnom; the Titans' prison

rendered_as.gloss: the place of eternal conscious torment

cases.what_happened: The KJV renders four distinct words - a neutral Hebrew term for the realm of the dead, a Greek term for the same, a Jerusalem rubbish-valley used as an image of judgment, and a verb drawn from Greek myth - with the single English word 'hell', which by 1611 already meant a place of eternal fiery punishment.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Produced the monolithic doctrine of hell in English-speaking Christianity, including the idea that the Old Testament teaches it. Psalm 16:10 read as 'thou wilt not leave my soul in hell' supplied the Harrowing of Hell and a clause of the Apostles' Creed. Revised versions transliterating Sheol and Hades separately are why annihilationist and universalist arguments gained traction from the 19th century onward.

first_attested.where: English tradition, fixed by the KJV

cases.caveat: This is the dataset's one multi-reference lexical case; treat each reference separately when analysing. The ASV's consistent transliteration makes it the best control version in this repository for the whole word-family. Geneva 1599 renders Psalm 16:10 'thou wilt not leaue my soule in the graue', not 'in hell' - so the correction the ASV is usually credited with had already been made in 1599 and was then undone by the KJV. Darby (1890) prints 'Sheol' and Rotherham (1902) 'hades' at Psalm 16:10, so the distinction the ASV is usually credited with was being made by several 19th-century translators. Wycliffe is deliberately NOT cited here: its Psalms follow Vulgate numbering, so Wycliffe Psalm 16 is the Hebrew Psalm 17.
scholarship: Alan E. Bernstein, The Formation of Hell: Death and Retribution in the Ancient and Early Christian Worlds (Cornell, 1993).

cases.title: rāqîa' -> 'firmament': the solid dome of heaven

source_term.gloss: a beaten-out expanse, from a root meaning to hammer metal thin

cases.what_happened: The Greek and Latin chose words emphasising solidity, and English followed. Modern versions render 'expanse' or 'vault', which softens the ancient cosmology the Hebrew probably does describe.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Cuts both ways, which is why it is here. The solid-dome reading fuelled the medieval and early modern Christian cosmology that made Galileo's case a theological crisis. The modern softening to 'expanse' is itself arguably a harmonising retranslation that conceals ancient Near Eastern cosmology from readers - an example of a translation drifting to protect a doctrine of scripture.
cases.caveat: Here the 'corrected' column is the disputed one: many scholars hold 'firmament' better conveys what the author meant, and 'expanse' is the tendentious rendering. A good test case for a dataset that should not assume newer is truer. Verified here: the JPS TANAKH 1917 reads 'firmament' alongside the KJV, so this is not a case where Jewish and Christian versions diverge.
scholarship: Paul H. Seely, 'The Firmament and the Water Above', Westminster Theological Journal (1991).
Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11 (Fortress, 1984).

cases.title: Zechariah's parallelism read as two animals

source_term.gloss: on a donkey, that is, on a colt, the foal of a she-donkey (synonymous parallelism: one animal)

rendered_as.gloss: on a donkey and on a colt (two animals)

cases.what_happened: Hebrew poetry restates the same thing in different words. Matthew's citation takes the two clauses as naming two animals, and his narrative then has the disciples bring both and place garments on them - a detail absent from Mark, Luke and John, each of which has one colt.
cases.doctrinal_impact: A standard exhibit in debates over gospel harmonisation, biblical inerrancy and the evangelists' use of the Septuagint. Whole apologetic literatures exist to reconcile Matthew 21:7 with the parallel accounts, and the case is a fixture in arguments about whether New Testament authors read the Old Testament with technical accuracy.
cases.caveat: A minority holds Matthew understood the parallelism perfectly well and reports two animals for reasons of his own. Verified here, and it reshapes the case: at Matthew 21:5 every English version renders two clauses, because Matthew's Greek has two. The versions only diverge at 21:7, where the KJV, NRSV and NET all read 'he sat on them' and the NIV alone writes 'for Jesus to sit on'. The NIV's rendering is a harmonisation rather than a correction, so 'corrected' is a label of convenience here - treat this case as a study of how versions handle an awkward text, not of who got it right.
scholarship: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, The Gospel According to Saint Matthew (ICC, T&T Clark, 1988-97).

cases.title: eudokias -> 'good will toward men'

source_term.gloss: among people of [God's] favour (genitive)

rendered_as.form: ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία / good will toward men
rendered_as.gloss: and good will toward all people (nominative)

transmission_chain: Greek NT (genitive in the oldest MSS)
cases.what_happened: A single final sigma separates the readings. The genitive, supported by the oldest manuscripts and by a Qumran parallel idiom, restricts the peace to those God favours. The nominative universalises it.
cases.doctrinal_impact: The best-known Christmas text in English proclaims a different message depending on one letter: universal goodwill toward humanity, or peace to an elect. The KJV reading shaped the sentimental Christmas of the English-speaking world; the critical reading has been read as supporting election.
cases.caveat: Strictly a textual variant that then forces a translation choice. The Vulgate sides with the critical text here, which makes it a useful counterexample to any assumption that the Latin always follows the Byzantine.
scholarship: Bruce M. Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd ed. (UBS, 1994), on Luke 2:14.
Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Gospel According to Luke I-IX (Anchor Bible, 1981).

cases.title: pasa graphē theopneustos: 'all scripture is inspired' or 'every inspired scripture'

source_term.gloss: ambiguous: 'every scripture is God-breathed and useful' or 'every God-breathed scripture is also useful'

rendered_as.form: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable

cases.what_happened: The Greek has no verb; where the reader supplies 'is' determines whether the sentence asserts that all scripture is inspired or presupposes inspiration and asserts usefulness. The Revised Version chose the second, the KJV and most modern versions the first.
cases.doctrinal_impact: The single most cited verse for biblical inspiration and, in the 19th and 20th centuries, for inerrancy. When the Revised Version printed 'Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable' the outcry was immediate, because the attributive reading appears to allow that some writings called scripture are not inspired. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy leans on the predicative reading.

first_attested.where: ambiguity is original to the Greek

cases.caveat: Labels inverted on purpose: the majority of grammarians favour the predicative reading the KJV has, so here the older version is the better one and the revision is the outlier. Included to keep the dataset from encoding a 'newer is truer' bias. Verified here: only the English Revised Version carries the attributive reading; the NRSV reverted to 'All scripture is inspired by God', so the 1881 revision stands alone against every other version in this repository. The attributive reading is not an 1881 novelty: Tyndale 1526 reads 'all scripture geve by inspiracion of god is proffitable', which is the construction that caused an outcry when the Revised Version printed it 355 years later. Geneva 1599 has the predicative 'the whole Scripture is giuen by inspiration of God'.
scholarship: I. Howard Marshall, The Pastoral Epistles (ICC, 1999) - on the predicative and attributive construals.

cases.title: harpagēsometha -> 'rapiemur' -> the Rapture

source_term.gloss: we shall be seized/snatched

cases.what_happened: Paul uses an ordinary verb. The Latin rapiemur supplied the English noun 'rapture', which from Darby and the Scofield Reference Bible onward named a distinct event: a secret removal of the church before a tribulation period.
cases.doctrinal_impact: An entire eschatological system, and one of the largest-selling fiction franchises in publishing history, rest on a noun the New Testament never uses. Pre-tribulational rapture theology shapes the politics of a substantial part of American evangelicalism, including attitudes to Israel and to environmental policy.

first_attested.where: Latin verb; the noun and doctrine from the 1830s

cases.caveat: No English version reads 'rapture' here, so this is reception rather than translation: the Latin made an English noun available and theology did the rest. Kept in the dataset because it shows a translation effect no verse-comparison alone would reveal.
scholarship: Ernest R. Sandeen, The Roots of Fundamentalism: British and American Millenarianism 1800-1930 (Chicago, 1970) - on Darby and the pre-tribulational scheme.

cases.title: 'camel' was really 'rope' (kamēlos / kamilos)

source_term.gloss: camel

cases.what_happened: The popular claim is that kamēlos and kamilos sounded alike in later Greek and that scribes wrote 'camel' for an original 'rope'. There is no independent evidence that kamilos was a real Greek word: its earliest appearance is in Cyril of Alexandria in the 5th century, and nearly every later occurrence is someone reporting it as a variant for this saying. The 'Needle's Eye Gate' in Jerusalem, the other standard escape hatch, is a medieval invention with no archaeological basis.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Its impact is as a domesticating move: both the rope and the gate stories convert a deliberately absurd image about the impossibility of rich people entering the kingdom into a merely difficult one. Tracking how often each appears in commentaries and sermons is a measurable index of how wealth has been preached.

first_attested.where: Cyril of Alexandria; gate myth from Theophylact or Anselm

cases.caveat: Included deliberately as a negative control. Every Greek witness in this repository reads kamēlos, which is exactly the point: an analysis pipeline that flags this verse as a mistranslation is finding something that is not there.
scholarship: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, The Gospel According to Saint Matthew (ICC, T&T Clark, 1988-97) - treats kamelos as secure and the rope variant as secondary.

cases.title: bere'shit bara' -> 'In the beginning God created'

source_term.gloss: ambiguous: 'In the beginning God created' or 'When God began to create'

rendered_as.form: ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν / in principio creavit / In the beginning God created

cases.what_happened: Bere'shit lacks the definite article and can head a temporal clause, giving a dependent construction - 'when God began to create, the earth being formless' - which presupposes pre-existing unformed matter rather than describing creation from nothing. Rashi read it this way; so do the NRSV and NJPS in their main text or notes.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Creatio ex nihilo, one of the load-bearing doctrines of Christian theology, is not stated in Genesis 1 under the dependent reading; it enters explicitly at 2 Maccabees 7:28 and is developed by the Fathers against Platonist matter. How Genesis 1:1 is rendered determines whether the doctrine is exegesis or inference.

first_attested.where: ambiguity original to the Hebrew; resolved by LXX and Vulgate

cases.caveat: Genuinely open. The absolute reading has strong defenders on grammatical grounds, and most English versions retain it. The dataset records the dispute. Verified here: only the NRSV and NAB carry the dependent reading in their main text. The NET's dependent reading lives in a translator's note, which this corpus does not store - an instance of the apparatus gap described in COVERAGE.md.
scholarship: Claus Westermann, Genesis 1-11 (Fortress, 1984).
Gordon J. Wenham, Genesis 1-15 (Word Biblical Commentary, 1987).

cases.title: Petros / petra: 'upon this rock I will build my church'

source_term.form: σὺ εἶ Πέτρος, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ
source_term.translit: su ei Petros, kai epi tautē tē petra
source_term.gloss: you are Petros (masc.) and on this petra (fem.) - two forms, one underlying Aramaic kepha

rendered_as.form: tu es Petrus, et super hanc petram
rendered_as.gloss: you are Peter and on this rock

cases.what_happened: In Greek the two words differ in gender and form, which allows a distinction between Peter and the rock. If Jesus spoke Aramaic he used kepha twice, with no distinction available. The Latin narrows the gap; English 'Peter'/'rock' widens it by hiding the shared root entirely.
cases.doctrinal_impact: The founding proof-text of the papacy, inscribed around the dome of St Peter's. Protestant exegesis distinguishing Petros from petra - the rock is Peter's confession, not Peter - depends on a Greek distinction that the underlying Aramaic probably did not have, while the Catholic reading depends on an Aramaic reconstruction not in the text. Both sides argue from a language other than the one the verse is written in.

first_attested.where: the Greek text itself; polemical use from the 3rd c.

cases.caveat: Not a mistranslation in any straightforward sense - it is a case where translation cannot preserve a pun, and the untranslatable residue became a confessional fault line. Verified here, and the result is blunt: the KJV, NRSV and NET obscure the wordplay exactly as the Vulgate and Douay-Rheims do, all reading 'Peter ... rock'. Only the two Peshitta-derived versions show it - the Aramaic Bible in Plain English reads 'you are Kaypha, and upon this stone', and the Lamsa Bible 'you are a stone, and upon this stone'. Confessional allegiance does not predict the rendering; source language does. Wycliffe is a third witness that preserves something of the pun - 'thou art Petre, and on this stoon' - where Tyndale, Geneva and the KJV all read 'rocke'/'rock'. The Peshitta is now present in Syriac itself, not only in English translation: at Matthew 16:18 it reads kepha twice, which is the Aramaic situation the whole Protestant-Catholic argument is reconstructing from a distance.
scholarship: W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, Matthew (ICC, 1988-97).
Oscar Cullmann, Peter: Disciple, Apostle, Martyr, 2nd ed. (Westminster, 1962).

cases.title: 'I hate divorce' or 'he who hates and divorces'

source_term.gloss: third person: 'if he hates, [and] sends away' - not first person 'I hate'

rendered_as.form: I hate putting away / I hate divorce
rendered_as.gloss: a divine declaration against divorce as such

cases.what_happened: The Hebrew verb is third person masculine singular, not first person, and the verse is grammatically difficult in every witness. Rendering it 'I hate divorce' requires emending or overriding the form. Recent versions moved to a third-person reading: the NIV 2011, the ESV and the CSB now render it roughly as 'the man who hates and divorces his wife ... covers his garment with violence'.
cases.doctrinal_impact: 'God hates divorce' became one of the most quoted sentences in Christian pastoral practice, church discipline and marriage counselling. Under the third-person reading the verse condemns a specific act of treachery against a wife rather than divorce as a category - a materially different pastoral text, which is why the recent revisions were contentious.

first_attested.where: ancient versions and the English tradition

cases.caveat: The Hebrew is genuinely corrupt or elliptical here; no reading is comfortable. Contested rather than settled, and a good stress test for any pipeline: within this repository the NIV, ESV and CSB carry the third-person reading while the KJV, NASB, NET and JPS 1917 carry 'I hate', so the same verse splits the modern versions down the middle rather than along the usual old/new line. Geneva 1599 reads 'If thou hatest her, put her away ... yet he couereth the iniurie vnder his garment' - the conditional third-person construction that the ESV and CSB adopted in the 2010s. The 'I hate divorce' reading is the innovation here, not the correction.
scholarship: Andrew E. Hill, Malachi (Anchor Bible, 1998).
David Instone-Brewer, Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible (Eerdmans, 2002).

cases.title: harpagmos: 'robbery' or 'a thing to be grasped'

source_term.gloss: did not regard it as something to be seized/exploited

rendered_as.form: thought it not robbery to be equal with God
rendered_as.gloss: did not consider equality with God to be theft

cases.what_happened: The KJV's 'robbery', following the Vulgate's rapinam, makes the verse assert Christ's rightful equality with God. The now-standard understanding, following Hoover's work on the idiom, is that harpagmos with hēgeomai means something to be taken advantage of - the verse is about Christ declining to exploit a status, not about whether the status was his by right.
cases.doctrinal_impact: One of the New Testament's central christological passages, argued over in every major controversy from Arianism onward. The KJV reading makes it a direct assertion of Christ's deity; the modern reading makes it a statement about self-emptying, which is why kenotic christology developed where it did.
cases.caveat: The lexical dispute is technical and the word is rare; 'majority' rather than 'strong' for that reason.
scholarship: Roy W. Hoover, 'The Harpagmos Enigma: A Philological Solution', Harvard Theological Review 64 (1971) - established the idiomatic sense now followed by most modern versions.

cases.title: kai theos ēn ho logos: 'the Word was God' or 'a god'

source_term.gloss: and the Word was God / was divine (anarthrous predicate nominative before the verb)

cases.what_happened: The predicate noun theos lacks the article. Colwell's rule and subsequent work on anarthrous pre-verbal predicate nominatives support a qualitative or definite sense, which is why virtually every translation reads 'was God'. The New World Translation's 'a god' takes the absence of the article as indefiniteness.
cases.doctrinal_impact: The single most contested verse between Trinitarian Christianity and Jehovah's Witnesses, and the reason John 1:1 appears in nearly every popular apologetics work on the Trinity. Also the standard teaching example for the limits of arguing doctrine from the Greek article.
cases.caveat: Graded contested because the grammatical question is real even though the consensus verdict is not close: 'a god' is rejected by the overwhelming majority of Greek grammarians. The New World Translation is not in this repository, so the disputed rendering cannot be quoted from it here - see the coverage report.
scholarship: Daniel B. Wallace, Greek Grammar Beyond the Basics (Zondervan, 1996) - on anarthrous pre-verbal predicate nominatives and the limits of Colwell's rule.
Raymond E. Brown, The Gospel According to John I-XII (Anchor Bible, 1966).

cases.title: porneia -> 'fornication' / 'unchastity': the exception clause

source_term.gloss: broad term for illicit sexual conduct; possibly incestuous or otherwise invalid unions here

cases.what_happened: Matthew alone attaches an exception to Jesus' prohibition of divorce, using porneia rather than the specific word for adultery, moicheia. Whether porneia means adultery, pre-marital unchastity, or unions invalid under Levitical kinship rules determines what the exception permits.
cases.doctrinal_impact: The basis of the divergence between Catholic canon law, which reads the clause as permitting separation but not remarriage, and Protestant practice, which generally permits remarriage after adultery. Millions of annulment and remarriage decisions turn on how one Greek noun is rendered.
cases.caveat: No rendering is agreed; 'corrected' here means 'preserves the ambiguity' rather than 'gets it right'.
scholarship: David Instone-Brewer, Divorce and Remarriage in the Bible (Eerdmans, 2002).
W. D. Davies and Dale C. Allison, Matthew (ICC, 1988-97).

cases.title: diakonos -> 'servant' when the officeholder is a woman

source_term.gloss: deacon/minister of the church

cases.what_happened: The same noun diakonos is routinely rendered 'deacon' or 'minister' when applied to men - including in the office list of 1 Timothy 3 - and 'servant' when applied to Phoebe. The Greek gives no basis for the distinction; Phoebe's title is further specified by a named church, which is the pattern for an office.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Kept the New Testament's one named deacon who is a woman out of view in English Bibles, with direct bearing on the debate over the diaconate for women in Catholic, Anglican and evangelical churches. A test case for translational consistency: the argument here is not about what a word means but about whether a version applies its own lexicon evenly.
cases.caveat: Some hold the office of deacon was not yet fixed when Romans was written, making 'servant' defensible. That defence has to explain the inconsistent handling of the same word within a single version, which is the analysable part and the reason this case is well suited to automated comparison. Verified here: the KJV, ESV, NASB, NET and CSB all read 'servant' at Romans 16:1 and 'deacons' at 1 Timothy 3:8; the NRSV and NIV read 'deacon' in both places.
scholarship: Carolyn Osiek and Margaret Y. MacDonald, A Woman's Place: House Churches in Earliest Christianity (Fortress, 2006).
Eldon Jay Epp, Junia: The First Woman Apostle (Fortress, 2005).

cases.title: andra ou ginōskō -> 'I am a virgin': a verb becomes an identity

source_term.gloss: I do not know a man (or: a husband) - present indicative active

cases.what_happened: Mary's only statement about her own sexual history is a verb phrase in the present tense: 'I do not know a man'. Sixteen English versions in this repository render it as a predicate noun - 'I am a virgin' - converting a statement about what she has not done into a statement about what she is. The Greek noun for virgin, parthenos (G3933), does occur in this chapter, at Luke 1:27, where the NARRATOR introduces Mary. It does not occur in her own speech. That contrast is computable from lexicon/ and is the cleanest evidence in the case.
cases.narrative_context: Mary is NOT yet pregnant when she says this, and the verb morphology settles it. At Luke 1:31 Gabriel says syllēmpsē, 'you WILL conceive' (V-FDI-2S, future). Mary's question at 1:34 uses estai, 'how WILL this be' (V-FDI-3S, future), with ginōskō in the present (V-PAI-1S). Gabriel's answer at 1:35 is future throughout: epeleusetai 'will come upon' (V-FDI-3S), episkiasei 'will overshadow' (V-FAI-3S). At 1:38 she consents with genoito, an aorist optative of wish - 'may it be'. Luke never narrates the conception itself; by Elizabeth's greeting at 1:42 she is pregnant. So her question precedes the conception, and cannot be a claim about any child's paternity. In Matthew there is no annunciation to Mary at all - 1:18 opens with her already 'found to be with child', and Mary never speaks anywhere in that gospel.
cases.doctrinal_impact: Shapes who is understood to be the witness to the virgin birth. Under 'I am a virgin', Mary appears to assert her own status, and the verse reads as her testimony. Under the Greek, she asks a question whose premise is that she has not had sex, and every assertion about the child's origin is made by someone else: the angel at Luke 1:35, the narrator at Matthew 1:18, the angel to Joseph at 1:20. The doctrine is unaffected; its attribution is not. The same verse is also the textual anchor for later claims about Mary's perpetual virginity, which the present-tense verb does not support on its own.

first_attested.where: 20th-century English versions; not in the KJV line

distinguish_from.note: Nothing here weakens the virgin birth, which Luke and Matthew assert plainly in their own voice. What it changes is who is said to testify to it. Mary never uses the word 'virgin' of herself and never says the child has no human father; at Luke 2:48 she calls Joseph 'your father', which is ordinarily read as legal or adoptive fatherhood.

cases.caveat: 'I am a virgin' is defensible as dynamic equivalence - it conveys the presupposition of her question accurately enough, and no one disputes that Luke means she has not had sex. Graded majority, not strong, for that reason. Note also that the versions split three ways rather than two: 16 use the identity noun; the KJV line keeps the literal 'I know not a man'; and a third group (CSB, NET, NAB, HCSB, ISV, GWT) keeps the verb but modernises it - 'I have not had sexual relations with a man'. That third group is arguably the best rendering and is filed here as corrected. A minority reads andra as 'husband' rather than 'man', giving 'I have no husband' (Weymouth, Twentieth Century), which shifts the sense toward her betrothed but unconsummated status.
scholarship: Joseph A. Fitzmyer, The Gospel According to Luke I-IX (Anchor Bible, 1981).
Raymond E. Brown, The Birth of the Messiah, 2nd ed. (Doubleday, 1993).

cases.title: 'his father' -> 'Joseph': scribes edit Joseph out of fatherhood

source_term.form: ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἡ μήτηρ
source_term.translit: ho patēr autou kai hē mētēr
source_term.gloss: his father and his mother

cases.what_happened: At Luke 2:33 the earliest witnesses read 'his father and his mother'; the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read 'Joseph and his mother'. The same substitution recurs at 2:43, where the critical text has 'his parents' (hoi goneis autou) and the TR again names Joseph. The direction of change is not seriously disputed: 'his father' is the harder reading, and no scribe defending the virgin birth would introduce it, while the motive for removing it is obvious.
cases.doctrinal_impact: A rare case where a scribal motive is legible from the change itself. Luke's own narrative calls Joseph Jesus' father without embarrassment - at 2:41 and 2:43 the parents are 'his parents', at 2:48 Mary says 'your father and I', and at 3:23 Luke adds his own hedge, 'as was supposed'. Scribes smoothed some of these and not others, so the KJV reader meets a Luke slightly more anxious about Joseph's status than Luke was. Relevant to Mariology, to perpetual-virginity debates, and as a demonstration that doctrinal pressure on the text is measurable rather than merely alleged.
cases.caveat: Two things complicate the neat story. First, the LATIN sides with the critical text: both the Clementine and Sixtine Vulgates read 'pater eius', so this is a Greek Byzantine development, not a Latin one - which cuts against any account that makes the Vulgate the villain of Marian readings generally. Second, Tyndale (1526) already has 'his father and mother', so the English tradition had the critical reading eighty-five years before the KJV adopted the Byzantine one. The repository's plain-text JSON carries no apparatus, so versions that footnote the variant are indistinguishable here from versions that print one reading silently.
scholarship: Bart D. Ehrman, The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture (Oxford, 1993) - the standard study of scribal alterations made for doctrinal reasons, which is the category this case belongs to.
